utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should say that today in Judge Mindua's absence we sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honour. I'm sorry to rise at this moment. However, I just have one very small submission to make to you. During the cross-examination of Witness T48 I tendered a UN document that was admitted, and I -- I realised thereafter that the same document had been admitted in the Galic case under seal and therefore pursuant to Rule 75 I ask that the exhibit P784 be similarly tendered under seal in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Request granted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, P 784 will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Witness T52 is protected. He has voice and image distortion -- or, rather, image distortion and a pseudonym. So could we have document 3D003986. Can it be shown all round, please, and to the witness. I wish to tender this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D277 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show the Judges this: During that period beginning with 1992, when there was combat, Nedzarici were attacked from what directions? Perhaps you can draw a couple of arrows.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Like this. Then from this area, from Mojmilo. From Stup.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, do you know what Hladnjaca or the cold storage is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I do. There was a slaughterhouse there as well. It was in Stup.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the spot where Hladnjaca was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I think this is Hladnjaca. Should I put it in a circle?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted you to do, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: This is the cold storage facility, this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any attacks from the direction of the airport? I suppose you can see it there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes. This is the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where were they attacking you from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Towards Nedzarici there were attacks from Dobrinja V and this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark it with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the beginning of the conflict, in terms of weapons what was it that your unit had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Infantry weapons, automatic and semi-automatic rifles, machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about the beginning of the conflict, whether you had any heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No, not at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You had no mortars in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Not at first, but later, yes, there were mortars close to the faculty of theology.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Three or four, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which brigade did you belong to? What was your unit in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The Ilidza brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who commanded the battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Battalion commander was Colonel Radojcic. No. The battalion commander was actually Svetozar Guzina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: That was Colonel Radojcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The 1st infantry unit. The 1st company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who commanded the company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: At first until I got wounded I was the commander of the company at Lukavica Road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you get wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: On the 28th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the time period during which you were absent from any combat activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I did not participate until October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to tender this map with its markings as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It will it be an admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please show a 65 ter photograph to the witness, the number being --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the number, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 02862 [Realtime transcript read in error "02860"] This is the photograph. However, in the transcript we have 02860 whereas I said 02862. This is the photograph, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on this photograph can you mark the separation line between the army of Republika Srpska and the 1st Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: That would be the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the place where you had worked before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Before the conflict I used to work here. Should I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, whenever I ask you about the photograph or any maps, you have to mark.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: This was the centre for the blind. This is where blind people work who had completed their training and education. I just wanted to add something else. The elementary school for blind children was here. It is this set of buildings. Upon completion of their primary education, they were able to stay at the centre for the blind where they also attended high school. After that, they would usually be employed by the centre for the blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The set of buildings you marked with the large circle, the largest building in the circle, what is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mark it separately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This elementary school for who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Blind children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mark it with an "S".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict what was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Our positions were in the school during the conflict, on the ground floor. That's where we slept as well and held positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was that building made of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: It is a solid building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I had in mind. What was the height in terms of floors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: It had the ground floor and two more floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict what was its use?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: During the conflict, on the ground floor we made trenches. We opened fire from those positions during an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know this, and maybe you can explain it to the Judges as well: Later in the conflict, and I mean the last year of it, what did things look like? Was the building in a somewhat different shape than shown here? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: That building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that question was slightly leading, in my submission. It would have been fine if -- if the counsel had just asked what did it look like during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. It was leading. You must avoid leading questions, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English interpretation may be leading. What I asked was what would -- the shape of the building in the last year of the conflict. That's what I asked. It says here "Did it appear any different."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If that's what you asked it isn't leading, but as it appeared in the transcript it was. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the shape of the building in the last year of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: It was destroyed in the last year of the war. The window -- windowpanes had burst. The roof was on fire, and it was riddled with bullets. Mortar shells landed on the building. It was almost completely destroyed, especially its upper parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the last year of the conflict concerning that building, where were you when you held positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: There were troops in the building on the ground floor throughout the war, including the last year. In the cellars, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, can you describe what these buildings are across the road from the separation line? If you can show them by neighbourhood. And did it look the same at the time of the conflict? Please, Witness, look at these high-rise buildings across the road from the separation line. Did they exist? Were they there at the time of the conflict from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: These buildings were there during the war. All these buildings were there. If you want me to mark them, this part here -- do you want me to mark them?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: This is Vojnicko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And behind that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: That's Alipasino Polje, those buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark what you have just circled with an "A"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Alipasino.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what you circled before that, mark it with a "VP", the letters"VP".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a building there that was a special threat to you during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tapuskovic. That is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you marked the separation line here. Right behind the separation line, that area, what did it look like during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: During the war this area looked the same, because there were garages here in this part which I haven't marked. Is that what you're asking me about, the part that I haven't marked? These were garages, and there was a sort of a market or shopping centre here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question might seem superfluous to you, but Vojnicko Polje and Alipasino Polje as you marked them, can you tell us who was in these buildings? Whose positions were on these buildings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, in my submission that is also a leading question, the suggestion being that there were positions in those buildings. If that's the case, then it should be elicited without leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't consider that leading, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said a little while ago, if I understood you correctly, that they were constantly shooting at you from these high-rise buildings. Who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: It was the Muslim army that was shooting at us from these high-rise buildings. The enemy army. And they overlooked us. They dominated above us, because you can see that where we were there were just ordinary houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And across on the other side of the separation line there are also some buildings there that are not very high. Who was in those houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The Muslim army, the enemy army. It was their positions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mark that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And to the right of that area right next to it, what was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: There was a parking lot and a shopping centre or a market before the war, and their positions were there also during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But please tell us what was there in terms of positions. What was conspicuous? What do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: There were paravan -- paravans [Realtime transcript read in error "caravans"]. There were containers, obstacles of various sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it says caravans whereas the witness said paravans. He also said containers and this did not enter the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the word. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a screen to conceal people from view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that area with a circle and put a "P" inside it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to tender this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now show the first photograph from the set labelled C, 00010.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on this photograph what is there behind the car, this light coloured car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Behind this car is a passageway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever use that passageway before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how long it is approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Ten or 12 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time of the conflict the area in front of the tunnel was under whose control? Whose army controlled it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The area in front of the tunnel was controlled by the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you looked through the tunnel -- well, we have better photographs, but at the other end of the tunnel do you recognise any buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see, it's the primary school for blind children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Between that school for blind children, which you've already mentioned, and the entrance to the tunnel, is that where these screens were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Another leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, possibly, but my objection -- not objection, was to clarify the time period that the witness is speaking to. I mean, I can do that in cross-examination. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, let the witness say what time this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What time period are you referring to? Does this refer to the last years of the war or -- well, please answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: If you are referring to the screens, the screens were there from the beginning to the end of the war. From the beginning of the conflict until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm especially interested in the other side. If you said that that house is the centre for the blind or the school for the blind, I'm interested in that area. Do you remember how long that area was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: You mean how far it was between the primary school and this part? Well, 200 or 300 metres, maybe more. I don't know. Around 200 or 300 metres, but I couldn't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. This is an exhibit, and I will not insist on tendering it now, or I won't deal with it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I could just ask for some clarification of this before we leave this picture. Witness, you said that -- that the area between this building and the school for the blind was the area in which the screens had been set up throughout the war, and my question to you would be do you know if the screens that were set up in that area, if those screens would obstruct the view from the passageway to the school of the blind? Were there any screens in the line of sight from the passageway to the facade of the school of the blind that would obstruct the direct view from one point to the other? Do you know this? Or if you don't know, then just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The screens were in this part, on this there side -- this here side towards the primary school for blind children. There was screens all the way there, and you couldn't see anything because of those screens. You couldn't see anything inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if you were standing where the photographer was standing, looking through the passageway towards the school of the blind, then what you're saying is that you would be unable to see the school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness T52, there's another question I'd like to put to you. Do you know when General Dragomir Milosevic became the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I think in August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me, in 1994 do you remember anything? How was 1994 in terms of combat? Can you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: 1994 was the quietest year, up until June sometime. It was quiet until mid-June. May, June, something like that. It was quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about 1994 when Dragomir Milosevic came to the command post of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Did anything happen in that year in relation to heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: That year the heavy weaponry was pulled back. There was an order that all heavy weaponry should be pulled back to 20 kilometres from the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened with the mortars that you said you had in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The mortars were taken from Nedzarici, from the theological faculty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And from the time that General Dragomir Milosevic arrived, how did that period look from July, August, September, October, November, December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: August, September, and October, or, actually, until the new year was a time of truce of a sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that, are you thinking of the area where you were living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know in Nedzarici about the existence of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: We knew that there was a tunnel that had been dug underneath the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And were you able to see from Nedzarici the entrance or the exit of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: From Kasindolska Street you could mostly see the exit to the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you observe during those months until the end of 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Until the end of 1994 we would see soldiers and civilians coming out of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to suggest anything. Soldiers and civilians, does that mean that they were coming out together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. They were coming out together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And from the places where you were, were you able to fire at them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: We didn't fire because there were always civilians together with the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me how long -- well, you said that there were no conflicts in Nedzarici in 1994. Can you please tell us what was the quietest period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The quietest period was in early 1995, up until May, June, something like that. I don't know exactly, but that's approximately the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Then the Muslim attacks were carried out on our positions along the whole length of the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did this culminate and what was it like? Can you describe that briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: It began in May, June. That's when the attacks at our positions began. There was continuous fire at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you two or three documents, and then I would more or less finish, but I want to see if you can tell us anything about that after what I heard from you. We're talking about document D159. Witness T52, can you please look -- well, we still don't have the English version. Can you please read aloud the heading and what it says below the heading, and can you please read items 1, 2, and 3 so that I could ask you something.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: "Command of the 12th Division --" should I read this "Strictly confidential. 02/2-2-182, Sarajevo, 4th of July, 1995. "Report on active combat actions." That's what BD means. Delivered to the command of the 1st Corps. "In regard to your --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please. Thank you. I told you. Can you now please read item 1, item 2, and item 3. Can you please read what it says in those three paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: "In the period from the 15th June to the 3rd of July, 1995, we fired from all types of weapons and heavy weapons at our disposal at over 300 VT of the enemy, firing points of the enemy." This is article 1, paragraph 1. 2: "Out of the firing at the firing positions, a large number were directly hit, out of which 36 firing positions at the PK the following things were destroyed: The firing points, bunkers where the enemy manpower was, the PAMs, the PATs, the infantry weaponry, preparations, dormitories and so on. 3: "During the past combat actions we estimate that we killed about 50 Chetniks and a much larger number has been taken out of action by being seriously or lightly wounded."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this correspond to the events that you described earlier during that period in June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you read here that it said in Article -- in paragraph 3 that 50 Chetniks were killed, what can you say in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Some soldiers were killed, but the majority of the casualties were all civilians inside the neighbourhoods, the settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at the last paragraph of this document. Can you please read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: "We estimate that the number of destroyed damaged firing positions, combat and non-combat MVs are greater because we fired at the same in conditions of limited advisability, at night, so we were not able to see everything absolutely."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when it says here that this was during the night, is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes. I said earlier that they fired at us during the day and during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Defence Exhibit D159.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, T52. My name is Manoj Sachdeva and I'm a lawyer for the Prosecution and I'm going to ask a you few questions today. Firstly let me ask you, you were wounded in February 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you go somewhere to convalesce, to recover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: It's true that I was wounded on the 28th of February, 1993. First I was admitted to the Zica hospital in Blazuj, after which I was transferred to the Zvezda hospital in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you were there for how long, can I ask you? Actually I understand that you returned to Nedzarici in October 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And Blazuj and Belgrade [Realtime transcript read in error "Nedzarici"] are far away from Nedzarici [Realtime transcript read in error "Belgrade"]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Blazuj is perhaps some six to seven kilometres from Nedzarici. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blazuj from Belgrade. That's what it says in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I asked from Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In any event those two locations Belgrade and Blazuj are far from Nedzarici; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I've just said Blazuj is six, almost seven kilometres from Nedzarici. Belgrade is in Serbia, and Blazuj is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you spent roughly eight months away from the area of Nedzarici in 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take when you said to the Court that the screens were erected throughout the conflict, that is 1992 to 1995, you clearly did not see the screens in those eight months when you were away. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: When I wasn't there I didn't see them, of course, but the screens were there or curtains, as you say, they were there from May 1992 until the 28th of February, 1993. I mean, they were there then, and I assume that they were there throughout the war. When I came back, the screens were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it's an assumption on your part. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that, because when I left the screens were there. When I came back the screens were still there. I don't know if they were the same screens, but they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you -- you were a company commander up until February 1993 in the 1st Battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how many battalions were there in Nedzarici? And I'm talking the period 1993 -- well, 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: There was only one battalion in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Didn't the battalion amalgamate with the Kasindolska battalion and become a larger battalion, is that right, sometime in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The Nedzarici battalion and the -- from the Kasindolska Street, and the battalion from the Kasindolska Street joined together and it was one battalion, because at the beginning of the war there was so much manpower that the two battalions were created. As the war continued some people left, some were killed, some were wounded, so the numbers went down. So then from the two, one battalion was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And within that battalion how many companies were there in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: There were three companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the three companies contained roughly how many soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Three to 400 soldiers. I don't know the exact number, but that's about the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I apologise, maybe my question wasn't precise enough. Are you saying that there were 300 soldiers per company or 300 soldiers in total?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: In total, in all three companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And apart from the barracks that you marked on the map -- you remember marking the barracks on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was there not a former -- a former JNA barracks somewhere in the centre of Nedzarici in addition to those barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: There was just one barracks in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you've mentioned that the school of theology was also controlled by the VRS in Nedzarici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And there were SRK soldiers in that location; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: There were SRK soldiers in the school for blind children from 1992 to 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I take it there were no civilians in the school for the blind children during the conflict, or at least 1994 to 1995, were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: There were no civilians. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And presumably your company or the companies in the Nedzarici battalion had company headquarters in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Each company had its own command in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And your company headquarters, shall I say, was -- was that adjacent to the Lukavica-Cesta road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes. That was about a hundred metres away from the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there were mortars positioned by the school of theology. You remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the mortars that you had or that the battalion had were 60-millimetre, 82-millimetre, and 120-millimetre mortars; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You also had howitzers and tanks at some time during the conflict in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: We never had howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Tanks? Did you have tanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: There was one tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you had direct fire weapons such as anti-aircraft artillery? Did you have that in Nedzarici during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: You mean the PATs. We didn't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So in Nedzarici, which you've already testified earlier today, which is a small area, we can agree that there with the school of theology, with the institute for blind children, with the three -- the companies that you mentioned, the three company headquarters, the barracks, the former barracks, and the military weaponry that you described, we can agree at least that there were a considerable amount of military facilities in that small area. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The barracks, and then there was the faculty of theology, the home for blind children. There was -- there were soldiers on duty at the school for the blind, the school for blind children, the same as ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you finished your answer, Witness. The same as?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Soldiers were on duty at the school for the blind in the same way as they were on duty at other places along the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I of course have nothing against all these questions being put, and of course questions can be put relating to matters throughout the entire war and conflict, but if a question is put to the witness, we need to have a specific time frame, time reference. Then the questions can be put once it is established exactly what time period they relate to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This appears to be a complaint common to both sides. What is the time frame? What time frame is this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was speaking generally now in terms of the time about the home for the blind. The Prosecutor asked me about the home for the blind, and I answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, you'd better try to get the witness to speak about a specific time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, my questions -- I prefaced my questions with the time frame of the conflict, and when I want to ask for specific time periods I will, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, when you came back after you were wounded, you told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it should be mentioned every time we're talking about key things, just like all the questions that were put regarding the heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you told the Court earlier that you returned to combat in October 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And for some reason I wasn't clear what you did when you returned. Were you -- did you take over the company command? Did you, in other words, return to your former position or did you take up another position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: When I returned, I was in the rear command of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And where were you positioned for that period? In other words, 1993 until the end of the war, where were you mostly positioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: In Kasindolska Street, the rear command of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it you were there constantly from 1993 until 1995? Well, let me ask you this: Did you go to the front lines in that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how often would you go to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Not very often. I went there because I had my compatriots there, fighters, cousins, neighbours. I would go and see them sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you say that you were working in the rear of the battalion, what exactly was your role, your military role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: My duties in the rear battalion service consisted mostly of procuring petrol. We didn't have electricity, so we were getting candles and fuel for burning, for the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say you went to the front lines, I take it that you used to visit the school for blind children. You used to visit your compatriots there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how often would you go, once a week, once every couple of days? From 1993 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be specific. Sometimes I would go once a week. Sometimes I wouldn't go for 15, 20 days. Sometimes I wouldn't go for a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you told the Court that the SRK, in other words, your colleagues, were on the ground floor of the school for the blind children. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that on top of the ground floor there was a first and a second floor. So in other words, there were three floors in that building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on the ground floor of the -- on the ground floor of the school for the blind you mentioned to the Court that the SRK soldiers would fire from that location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: In case of an attack, there would be firing from the basement. There would be firing at the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: T52, before the break we were talking about the school for the blind children, and you told the Court that the SRK would fire from the ground floor. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I take it they would fire into the area controlled by the ABiH. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's also correct, is it not, that the SRK were on the first and the second floor? They were also located on those two floors in the school for the blind children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that the first floor and the second floor were used by the SRK for observation purposes? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The first and the second floor, well, we didn't dare go up there since there were large windows there. As you could see for yourself in the photograph, you can see what the height of the buildings in Vojnicko Polje and Alipasino Polje are. They are far taller than that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, your evidence is that the first and second floor were not used by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to observe into ABiH territory. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Sometimes on occasion, but we didn't dare. We tried not to get killed. Therefore, we didn't move about the first and the second floor. People were not even thinking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So sometimes on occasion the SRK would go up to the first and second floors to observe territory of the ABiH. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Never on the second floor. No one dared to go there. On the first floor maybe somebody occasionally would go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, are you sure about that answer, that the second floor was never used - and I'm talking the period 1993 to 1995 - that the second floor was never used by the SRK to observe enemy territory? Are you sure about that answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes. I am sure that people did not dare go up to the second floor. I'm telling you for the third time. No one dared go up there because of their safety. The other buildings surrounding it were far higher and they didn't go -- they didn't dare go there, otherwise they would be seen from those tall buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, it's correct that you testified for the Galic case in October 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that when you commenced your testimony you read or you gave a declaration to tell the truth. Do you remember doing that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you remember being questioned by Defence counsel and then cross-examined by Prosecution counsel at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also recall that the -- the organisation or the set-up of the courtroom were as we see here. In other words, your answers were recorded by an official court reporter and translated by an official interpreter. Isn't that also right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I want to bring your attention to the cross-examination by the lawyer, Mr. Mark Ierace, and Mr. Ierace, at page 14070 on the 21st of October, asked you the question whether the SRK would use the first and second floor, and I'm going to quote your answer. You answered: "I also and likewise claim that the fire was opened from the ground floor and that the upper floors mostly were used to observe. I've just explained why we couldn't fire from the upper floors because there were tall buildings dominating and one could see everything through the windows." That was your answer. So what I'm suggesting to you is, Witness, is that the SRK did use -- or at least your answer in the Galic case was that the SRK used the second floor to observe enemy territory. Now, what do you say to that? What is your answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Witness. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said an a minute ago, sometimes people went up to the first floor. As for the second floor, they didn't dare. They tried to stay alive. I think that last time in the Galic case I said that the upper floor was used but maybe it turned out to be the upper floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Sachdeva, in the quotation from Galic it says the upper floors were used mostly, mostly, to observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and what I'm suggesting to the witness, and my questions have been limited to the -- the activity of observation, and so I'm not suggesting -- I'm not putting the question about firing at this point, but I'm simply suggesting to the witness that the upper floors, that includes the first and the second floors, were used by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to observe into enemy territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: This is what you said in the Galic case, and I want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I spoke when the -- I was not switched on. I was indicating that Mr. Sachdeva should yield to you since you're on your feet. What is it you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since we are putting this to the witness, it would be fair to mention page 13919, and the answer he provided upon Judge Riad's question. It is that page, lines 13 to 17. It would be fair to put that to the witness as well, in addition to the part referred to by my learned friend so as to put the question in its proper form and in order to gain an answer. In answering Judge Riad's question, I think this witness should be referred to the answer he gave at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That of course would be something that you could do in re-examination, but let us hear what that question was from Judge Riad, Mr. Sachdeva, and what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, my recollection on being on the Galic case was that there was -- Judge Riad was not a Judge on that case. It was Judge -- His Honour Judge El Madhi, His Honour Judge -- Presiding Judge Orie and His Honour Judge Nieto-Navia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us attend to the line rather than the Judge. What's the line that you wish to refer to in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know very well who presided. I said Judge Orie, and the page is 13919, lines 13 to 17 in the English transcript. If need be, my colleague can read that aloud, read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you ready, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have the -- I have the part of the transcript that my learned counsel refers to, and my submission is that learned counsel can put that this to the witness in re-examination. Mr. Ierace, in my submission, established in cross-examination that there were three floors, that is, the ground floor and two other floors, the first and second floor, and the answer the witness gave to Mr. Ierace, in my submission, is what I've read out, that the upper floors are used to observe enemy territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. You put it in re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, let's start this way: Do you agree that the school for the blind children had three floors? In other words, a ground floor, a first floor, and a second floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you refer to the upper floors, the upper floors refer to the first and second floor, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So in your answer to Mr. Ierace as to whether the SRK used the upper floors, that is the first and second floor, to observe enemy territory, you were referring to the upper floors when you said they used those floors to observe, the first and second floor. I'm not talking about firing. I'm talking about observation. Did the SRK use the second floor to observe enemy territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: As I said, the uppermost -- no. The upper floor, the first floor, was used to observe. The second floor -- well, maybe one of our people would go up there on occasion to observe. Otherwise, we didn't dare go up there for the reasons of safety. Maybe some people may have gone up there in the evening or when there was a lull, but as for the second floor being used, very few people dared to go up there. Well, I said the upper floor because I know what was happening in that part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. So you accept that on occasion and sometimes the second floor would be used by soldiers of the SRK to observe. You accept that possibility, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Sometimes and briefly only. To go up there quickly, have a look around, and immediately go back down since it wasn't safe to be up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection in the sense that this is irrelevant. Even if someone did go up there, and we will go back to the transcript to see whether there was anyone on the second floor at all, in our view even if it was so, it is still irrelevant in our position, because there was no mention of any firing from the roof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- I submit that it is extremely relevant as to whether the SRK were on the second floor of the school for the blind children and my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I would think so myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, witness, let's just go back to where we agree. You accept that there was a possibility, there was a possibility that the SRK would sometimes go up to the second floor to observe enemy territory. You accept that as a possibility, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: As I said, maybe someone went up there seldom because they didn't go up and there stay there. It was very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And they were to go up there to the second floor because the vantage point or the observation from that second floor was -- how should I put it? It was an effective place to observe enemy territory being that it was the highest floor in the building. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: One could go and have a short look, but to efficiently observe enemy territory among all those buildings, given their size that was no use. But still I maintain that no one dared to stay there for a long time but if they did go up there, they would return very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, please just try and answer the question I'm asking you. I'm not asking you as to whether it was a useful purpose, a useful thing to do or not. I'm simply putting to you that from the second floor of the school for the blind children the view to those buildings that you speak about, the view to enemy territory was superior on the second floor than it would have been on the first floor. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's also correct, is it not, that because of the superior view or the superior observation point of the second floor, the SRK soldiers would fire from that floor into enemy territory. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you tell the Court that the SRK were firing from the ground floor. You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that it is absurd to say that the SRK would fire solely from the ground floor and not from the second floor where the commanding view was superior. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: This is what I have to say to that: How can anyone open fire from the second floor when surrounding that building were the buildings at Vojnicko Polje and Alipasino Polje? And the windows were facing Alipasino Polje. How can anyone open fire, because it can be observed easily. You can see every shot being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The building would have been observed by the surrounding buildings whether you were on the second or the ground floor. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: It could have been observed, but there is a great difference being on the second floor and on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about the firing coming from these apartment blocks, and I will move to that photograph in a moment. I take it that when there was firing the SRK would return fire. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the SRK would return fire by the use of mortars and infantry weapons; that is right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Mortars. I don't know when. It must have been in consultation with the higher command as to when mortars would be used. As for infantry weapons, when the Muslims would open fire, we fired back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But mortars were used against apartment blocks, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Mortars were used in case of attack and in agreement with our superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With a question like this, the witness should be asked as to when that happened, having in mind the indictment and the time encompassed in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. He's already said he didn't know when.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that the launching of mortars or the deployment of mortars at these apartment blocks is an ineffective use of military weaponry. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also agree that the -- the apartment blocks that you -- remember you marked on the photograph the apartment blocks in Vojnicko Polje and Alipasino Polje. Do you remember marking those apartment blocks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in 1994 and 1995, civilians lived in those apartment blocks, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I don't know whether any civilians were living there at the time. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you accept --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: In Vojnicko Polje, the buildings that were close were not inhabited by civilians, and we couldn't see any. As for the rear, well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let's have this photograph up on the screen. I think it's Defence Exhibit 279. Sir, let's concentrate on the apartment blocks where you have in the circle that says VP, and the -- the apartment blocks towards the left-hand side, you see those apartment blocks there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Just a moment. These ones here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's just the apartment blocks just to the left of the letters VP. Those are the blocks I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, civilians lived there, didn't they, from 1994 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Most likely, but I didn't see them. Most likely they did. They had to live somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, sir, you would agree with me that -- well, let's first -- do you have any knowledge about mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Do you -- do you mean the mortars that were down there --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I apologise --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: -- by the monastery in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, I apologise. My question wasn't precise enough. I'm suggesting to you that -- well, you agree with me that mortars are -- the primary purpose of mortars is to kill and maim personnel? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, sir, you would agree with me that the firing of mortars at these buildings would cause civilian casualties, would they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: If there were people there, then, yes, there would have been casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also agree that where the -- where you have placed the letter "A", in other words, Alipasino Polje, you agree with me that from 1994, 1995, civilians lived in those apartment blocks, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Most likely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's correct that the SRK from Nedzarici in 1994, 1995, would fire mortars into that area, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: In 1994, 1995 from Nedzarici? Well, when the heavy weapons were withdrawn, they were withdrawn from Nedzarici. That was when the mortars were withdrawn from Nedzarici at the monastery when the order arrived, and they left Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware that in this case we have evidence that -- that after the total exclusion zone agreement was signed that the -- that General Milosevic attempted to defeat or to deviate from that agreement by concealing the heavy weapons and not handing them over to UNPROFOR? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You are -- well, let's talk about the commander of Ilidza brigade, Vladimir Radojcic. He was a commander, was he not, from 1993 -- well, 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you aware that in the summer of 1995 the commander of Ilidza brigade frequently requested the supply of heavy weaponry, including 120-millimetre mortars, 82-millimetre mortars and modified air bombs? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that in 1994, 1995, in Nedzarici there were indeed mortars positioned there, and they were indeed used and fired into enemy territory. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I'm telling you there weren't any mortars in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about the screens. Do you remember talking about the screens and the containers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that you accept that the screens and containers were set up in order to prevent civilians from being hit by sniper fire. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I agree that containers and screens were set up to protect civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And they were set up to protect -- and they --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I actually interrupted your answer. What was the last thing you said, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: That screens were set up and containers were set up to protect civilians from bullets and from being seen, so that they couldn't be seen passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Because if they were seen, they would be fired at, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The screens and containers were set up both because of the civilians and also because of the soldiers, so they could pass by. That's how it was everywhere. Of course if one saw a soldier passing by, one would have to shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what I'm putting to you, sir, is that if a civilian was not protected and if a civilian could be seen, that civilian would be shot at, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No. I have just said -- I said when Mr. Tapuskovic was questioning me about the tunnel, the passage. It was both civilians and soldiers who went there, and we didn't shoot at all because there were civilians among the soldiers, and now you're asking me the same thing again. It was an order from the command, and also it was what people thought. Why would they shoot at civilians? Civilians weren't to blame for anything. Women, little children, old people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say the tunnel, the passage, I presume you're talking about the tunnel under the airport.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you're saying that because there were soldiers and civilians, no fire would be targeted at that location. That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying, and that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But at the same time, at the same time you have testified that mortar fire and infantry fire would be fired at those apartment blocks where civilians were living. Didn't you just say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: When did I say that? I didn't say that at all that mortar fire was opened on the blocks of houses where civilians lived. It was only at the separation lines that fire was opened. Why would anyone fire into the settlement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: At least our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you not testify in chief, in examination-in-chief that the ABiH would be firing from those apartment blocks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: From the first blocks fire was opened. And what was deeper inside, you say shells, but who would be crazy enough to fire shells into the settlement? Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You also said that if the order came down from the command that mortar fire would be used to retaliate at those locations. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now -- well, let me just ask you one question. Actually, I'm going to move on to a photograph. If we could have the photograph that was - the photograph of the passageway. I can't remember the exhibit number offhand. It's the one of the passageway from the site visit. I think it's the Chamber's Exhibit number 10. Witness, you remember seeing this photograph in examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I want you to look -- well, you told the Court that the building that you can see through the passageway, that that building is the school for the blind children. That's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, sir, you would agree with me that from where this photograph is taken, in other words, from where the car is, there is a line of sight from the school of the blind into the passageway. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I take it that you -- you don't remember what you were doing on the 24th of October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so I take it that you don't remember whether there was a screen or not at that location on the 24th of October. That's not something that you can remember, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Listen, in every passage, on every street there was screens and obstacles. That's a hundred per cent certain. Wherever people passed from 1992, and I'm talking about the period I was there, from October there were always screens there until the end of the war. Screens and obstacles and containers in the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I appreciate your answer but you're not answering my question. I'm suggesting to you that you do not remember seeing a screen on the 24th of October at that location, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No, I don't, but I'm telling you there was screens everywhere. Of course I can't remember. How many years have elapsed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he said he didn't remember whether it was the 24th of October, but he did say from October onwards. So I don't know why the same questions are being asked again and again. He said up to 1993 -- or from 1993, and from October until the end of the war. He's already said that. If he has to repeat it several times, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva, what's the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May I just respond? That's -- the question that -- I asked a very specific question, whether the witness remembers or not, and his answer was he doesn't remember. And I'm satisfied with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness, are you aware that in this case a civilian came and testified under oath in this court about the targeting of one of his friends in that passageway from the school for the blind, are you aware of that, on the 24th of October 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In fact, this person who testified was a civilian living in those apartment blocks. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, sir, I suggest to you that after that incident it was then that screens were erected, because the SRK were firing at civilians in that area. Isn't that why the screens were erected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: When was that incident, the 24th of October? What year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: And that the screens were erected only after that? No, they were erected in 1992, and they were there until the end of the war, not after that incident where that person, I don't know who, was killed. It wasn't after that. I keep telling you. The screens were there all the time throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, Witness, is it your evidence that the SRK did not fire from the school for the blind into ABiH territory at civilians in 1994, 1995? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The orders from the higher command, the brigade command, were that there was to be no shooting at civilians, and there was no shooting at civilians. There was no shooting at civilians. People didn't want to kill women, children, elderly people. There was no question of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you testified that you would visit the school for the blind once a week; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I said once a week or sometimes once a fortnight or once a month. That's what I said. I didn't say only once a week. I remember what I said very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. And therefore you don't know, do you, during the times that you weren't there, you don't know if the SRK would fire from the school for the blind into civilians -- at civilians in ABih territory. You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Well, listen, I just said there were orders. If I wasn't there, how could I know, but I doubt it because there was strict orders that there was to be no shooting at civilians. It was not allowed to shoot at civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, it's an assumption on your part that civilians were not targeted. That's all I'm asking you to agree with.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Well, that's my assumption and I know that, because there was an order. I'm telling you again there was an order from the brigade command that there was to be no shooting at civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to go into private session, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, Witness, I'm going to ask you some questions about this person, but please don't mention his name because he is, like you, protected. Now, he gave testimony in this case and also in the Galic case that there would be -- that the international community would make allegations against the SRK in Nedzarici for things, for things that were done. Are you aware of those allegations?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This identifies the witness. First the identity of the witness was revealed to this witness, and then the protected witness, he was protected, and now he is no longer a protected witness because this witness now knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was done inadvertently. So we have to ensure -- Witness, Witness, are you hearing me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are not reveal the name that has just been given. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. It was indeed inadvertent, and I -- in an attempt to be fair to put the name to the witness, I asked that question. So I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you, when you were in Nedzarici in 1993 to 1995, were you aware of allegations by the international community and by the United Nations that the Bosnian Serb army in Nedzarici would be firing at civilians within the ABiH confrontation line? Are you aware of those allegations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I don't know what the international community said. I'm not aware of that. When I listened to the radio, we usually switched on the radio using generators, and very often they would say that civilians had been killed by a shell from Nedzarici when no shell had been fired nor did anyone hear a shell being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you aware that your battalion, in other words, the 1st Battalion, your battalion commander, at least it was recorded by the United Nations that he admitted to United Nations personnel in July 1994 that there was indeed sniping from the school for the blind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. As far as I know, there was no sniper activity from the centre for the blind or the school for the blind. This is the first time I've heard of such a thing. And I don't know about the commander of the 1st Battalion admitting that there were such activities. This is the first time I've heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You're saying to the Court that today is the first time that allegations were put -- that you have heard of allegations that the SRK was firing, sniping from the school for the blind? Is today the first time you're hearing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Never was there a sniper in the centre for the blind. We didn't have snipers there. We had rifles, and that was all. It was all just small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: With respect, Witness, that's not the answer to my question. I'm asking you is today the first time that you are hearing of allegations that the SRK would fire, whether by rifles or other weapons, at civilians from the school for the blind. Is today the first time you're hearing that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the first time, but certainly no shots were fired from a sniper from the centre for blind children. I never said that no shots were fired from the centre for blind children, because if there was an attack, we would have to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the shots that you're talking about firing from the centre for the blind, those shots were fired from the ground floor. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you were aware, are you, of an anti-sniping agreement that was signed in August 1994, in fact, signed by General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you agree with me that the anti-sniping agreement was promulgated because civilians were being killed within ABiH territory by the SRK. You agree that was the reason for the anti-sniping agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
