utterances.text: The agreement was signed. I suppose it was signed by both sides, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the army of Republika Srpska. It wasn't signed just by General Milosevic. It was signed by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. That's what an agreement entails. So with respect to General Milosevic and with respect to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, it was signed, it was promulgated because the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were firing at civilians inside the city, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: In my opinion that agreement was signed so that neither the army of Republika Srpska nor the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina would fire. You keep telling me that the reason the agreement was signed was because the army of Republika Srpska was firing at civilians of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Very well then. So you would agree with me then that the agreement was signed because -- in other words, to prevent the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from firing at civilians, and similarly, to prevent the ABiH from firing at civilians on the other side. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Most probably the agreement was signed because both sides were firing at civilians, but who was shooting, I'm telling you only about the area I was in. I don't know about areas where I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you agree with me that the agreement was signed because the SRK were firing at civilians in ABiH territory, and the ABiH were firing at civilians on SRK territory? You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Most probably that's why the agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also agree, do you not, that after the agreement was signed it was routinely violated by members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? In other words, the sniping of civilians inside the city continued, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I don't know, but I can assert that in the area where I was there was no sniper activity. And how could we violate an agreement if it was signed and if we had orders? We were soldiers. We obeyed our superior commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so after August 1994, it's your testimony that there was never firing from Nedzarici into the city where civilians were targeted. That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Well, you were just talking about snipers. Are you now referring to snipers --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Because then you talked about the agreement. As far as I know, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the record, I was referring to snipers or fire from small-arms fire. And your answer is no; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: As far as snipers are concerned, my answer is no. And I'm saying that there was no firing on civilians, because there were orders from the brigade command, the battalion command that there was to be no shooting on civilians. And I repeat, we were soldiers and we obeyed all the orders of our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you're aware that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I'm not saying that, but 90 per cent orders were respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you -- in 1994 and 1994, you were aware that the United Nations had a protection force in Sarajevo? You were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No [as translated].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I understand that you said yes. The transcript -- although the interpretation was no. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you are similarly aware that the -- the United Nations Protection Force also had a subdivision known as United Nations Military Observers. You must have come across United Nations Military Observers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you are aware that the main goal or the main purpose of the United Nations Military Observers were to monitor the cease-fires, to ensure that the -- the agreements such as the TEZ were adhered to and to investigate civilian casualties by sniper fire and mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And are you also aware that within -- at least in the vicinity of Nedzarici there was a UN presence, wasn't there, in the vicinity of Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, it was down there on the road, on the Kasindol Road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I've already put it to you that the battalion commander had, in July 1994 admitted to a United Nations Military Observer that sniping took place from the school for the blind children. So in other words, your commander or colleagues in Nedzarici would meet with the United Nations Military Observers. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: They probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for 65 ter 02002 to be brought up, please. In a moment, Witness, you're going to see a document on your screen. I understand there is a -- oh, yes. Excellent. Now, Witness, if you look at the screen on your -- on the right-hand side, you will see that this is a United Nations document from the 8th of September, 1994. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, on the right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if the right-hand side could be scrolled down, please, or perhaps it goes down to the next page, but for now if it could be scrolled down. Actually, no, it needs to go on the next page. So, Witness, this is the next page of that document, and it corresponds to the English version which is on the left-hand side, and you will see -- you will see that the subject matter is violations of the Sarajevo anti-sniping agreement. Did you see that on the first page or do I need to go back to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: We need to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, if you look where it says Predmet, you would agree with me that this subject matter is entitled violations of the Sarajevo anti-sniping agreement, yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And now we can go on to the next page. And if you see this document lists violations of this agreement, and the first one you'll see on the 14th of August, there was a violation of the agreement where there was sniping near the Holiday Inn. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on the 22nd of August, 1994, it says: "Bosnian wounded by Serb [Translation read in error "sniper"] sniper from the BSA [Translation read in error "Serbian"] side in Nedzarici."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so is it still your evidence that there was no firing from the Nedzarici into ABiH territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Not with a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So this official report by the United Nations in your view is incorrect; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes. Not with a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you say not with a sniper, do you also mean not with small-arms fire? Is that what you also mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: What I mean are snipers. You're speaking about a sniper, and it says here in August civilian wounded by Serb sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, maybe we're now misunderstanding each other, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that -- Mr. Tapuskovic -- just a moment, please. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the translation is not clear. Perhaps the translation from English is ambiguous. I don't know how it is in English. Perhaps that is confusing the witness, because it says "Serb sniper wounded Bosnian on the side of the army of Bosnian Serbs." So it can mean that somebody on the side of the Bosnian Serb army was injured. That's what it says in the Bosnian translation, and that it was -- that somebody was injured on the Serbian side. There were Bosnians here on that side and on the other side there were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the translation appears to be wrong, and actually the -- the exhibit in its original language English is instructive, so I can read what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps that can be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Read what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The timing is the same, 221830 B August: "Bosnian wounded by Serb sniper from the BSA side at Nedzarici," and then it gives a grid reference. That's what it says in the original language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation is not clear. In Nedzarici. Somebody was wounded in Nedzarici. That is what it comes out as and that is how the witness understands it and that's how it's stated. I would need the help of the interpreters to clear that up. Where is that point? Let us discuss that. Where is that elevation, please? Where is that elevation? If that elevation is in Nedzarici then there is no dispute that it is somebody who was a casualty in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the English, which is the original, says "at Nedzarici."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here "in Nedzarici," too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't see the significant difference. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, what the English document says is that a Bosnian was wounded by a Serb sniper from the BSA, that is the Bosnian Serb army, I suggest to you, at Nedzarici. So my question still stands. Is it still your evidence that there was no sniping or small-arms fire from Nedzarici at civilians in ABiH territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I assert that there were no snipers at that time. That is what I assert. Infantry weapons at civilians, that I don't know because there was a ban on firing at civilians. I cannot assert that 100 per cent, but I assert regarding snipers 100 per cent that there was no firing from Nedzarici at civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you accept the possibility that there was firing at civilians from infantry weapons, in other words, rifles, M-48s? You accept that possibility, do you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: It's possible that somebody did fire, but there was a strict order not to fire at civilians, and believe me that we really did listen to our command. We had to listen to them. And this is the tenth time that I'm repeating that we obeyed our command that there was an order not to fire, and there was no fire. I don't know. Perhaps there were exceptions. I cannot claim that there weren't right now, but I am telling you how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, when you returned -- when you returned to Nedzarici I understand you were in the rear services?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And for the preponderance of the time you spent in Nedzarici that was at the rear. In other words, not on the front lines. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And -- and when you went to the front lines, in other words, when you went to visit the school for the blind children once every 15 days, as you said, I take it you were not involved in combat activity. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No. I went there to see friends, colleagues, cousins.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it is correct that you were not involved in combat activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P793, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And may I just have a moment to confer with my colleague, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. [Prosecution counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, my last -- my last topic, which won't take very long. You have -- in your evidence you've referred to the army on the other side as the Muslim army. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You know, do you not, that the -- the army on the other side of the confrontation lines had -- at some point during the conflict had as its chief of staff somebody called Stjepan Siber, who was a Bosnian Croat. You know that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I had heard of that, but to tell you the truth I wasn't really that interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you must have heard that Jovan Divjak was at some point the commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You must have heard that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's not correct, then, is it that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a Muslim army. That's not right, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was 90 per cent Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was an amalgamation of all ethnicities. All ethnicities participated in that army; is that right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: There were members if you count the HVO. That was the Croatian army, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croat army comprised of Croats, and the Bosnian army was 90 per cent Muslim, and there were the odd Serbs, Croats, or others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also are aware that within the confrontation lines in Sarajevo, in other words, within the city, all ethnicities remained there during the war. In other words, Bosnian Muslims, Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs remained inside the city of Sarajevo, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. What do you mean the pre-war people who lived there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you, sir, is that during the conflict, in other words, from 1992 through to 1995, inside the city of Sarajevo, in other words, inside the area controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were Bosnian Serbs, Bosnian Croats, and Bosnian Muslims living there during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: -- it is sure, for sure -- may I finish? For sure that there weren't more than 5 or 6 per cent of Serbs, and there were those who didn't get out in time. They were unable to leave. And the Croats joined their own HVO, because there was an HVO in Sarajevo as well. Practically all Croats were in their HVO. The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was 90 per cent plus comprising Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness, I appreciate your information, but in fact it's not what I have asked you. You just -- I just want you to agree with me, for whatever reason and for whatever percentage, there were Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks living in Sarajevo, inside the city during the conflict. That is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And therefore, you also agree that whether you or Serb or a Croat or a Bosniak, if you were a civilian living in Sarajevo, you were subjected to artillery fire, mortar fire, sniper fire on a regular basis, especially in the period 1994 to 1995 from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Let me tell you. If you're thinking of the centre of town and what happened in the centre of town, if there was snipers, mortars, what I'm telling you now is about the area where I was. There were no snipers or mortars there. It's another thing what the propaganda and TV did in Sarajevo and how they presented this and that, including from Nedzarici, from here, from there. There was firing from everywhere, according to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just one last question. The UN document that I showed you -- remember the UN document a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is it your view that this UN document is also propaganda?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. If the UN wrote that, but that document is not clear to me. Serbs, non-Serbs, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of the cross you were asked about what was happening to the people in Sarajevo under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but all right. Please tell me, Nedzarici, where are Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Nedzarici is located at the foot of Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where is Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Grbavica is below Trebevic, at the foot the Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor asked you about how a lot of Serbs stayed behind in Sarajevo. First of all, do you know if they were able to leave Sarajevo at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The Serbs who left in time left. Those who didn't leave in time, up until June or May 1992 they had to stay in the town of Sarajevo because they were not allowed to leave. And then on television they would say how Serbs are living there, but a small number stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please explain to us what was happening in Nedzarici? Was it known what was happening to the Serbs in Sarajevo in the area under the control of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva. May I remind counsel that the practice to be followed is that if a counsel is questioning and the other counsel stands up to make a point, then the counsel questioning should stop immediately and hear the point which the other counsel wishes to make. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, upon listening to the question, I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you find out in Nedzarici what was happening to Serbs who had stayed in Sarajevo, in the parts that were under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because you were in Nedzarici and in Sarajevo but in areas under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. What happened to Serbs that were in the areas of Sarajevo that were under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, I understood your question. Some Serbs who left early -- later, using some connections or who managed to get across, would speak about how Serbs in the Muslim parts under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had a hard time of it, that they had to go to dig trenches. Wherever it was difficult they were put forward. They had to go to areas where there was combat, that civilians, men and women, had to go in for interrogations, that they were left in prisons, that they were beaten and mistreated and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did anything worse happen to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: They were beaten. Some said that they didn't get any humanitarian aid or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, two -- two points on this line of questioning. Firstly, in my submission it does not strictly arise out of cross-examination. My question to the witness was with respect to the -- the suffering of all ethnicities, in other words, civilians in Sarajevo from artillery fire and sniper fire, number one. Number two, in my respectful submission, counsel has to provide a basis for the witness's knowledge. Again of course I accept that hearsay evidence is admissible; however there is no time period reflected here. There is no information as to how the witness has come about this information, who told him certain things, and in my submission this -- this evidence is not only to be accorded little weight but also unreliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How does it arise, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva wanted to say that the town of Sarajevo in the parts that were under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was his question, that that is where Serbs, Croats, and Muslims remained there voluntarily to live together, but I think that it is logical to seek an explanation about the circumstances in which the Serbs who stayed out of a hundred-plus thousand, the ones that stayed, what these people experienced and what the witness knows about that. So this directly arises from the questions by my learned friend Mr. Sachdeva because it seemed that they stayed there to continue living there because that is what they wanted, but actually they couldn't leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, my questions in my submission were very clear and there was no suggestion as to the reasons why they stayed. I simply wanted the witness to confirm that there were members of all ethnicities in Sarajevo, and he did, and that's all there is to it. I didn't go into the reasons why they stayed there. I didn't go into the reasons why they allegedly could not leave, and so in my submission this material could have been elicited in examination-in-chief if indeed counsel wanted to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. You may ask the question, Mr. Tapuskovic, but let us move on quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find out what was happening to people other than what you've said, who stayed in Sarajevo and did that have any significance as far as you were concerned in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The people I left, I mentioned earlier what they told us. There were killings there too. I am going to give you an example. Rade Grahovac, he was killed and his sons left, they came to Serb territory in 1994. Immediately after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't need that. We have had enough evidence on this. What's your other point now, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other point, Your Honours, is what the witness found out, was that of any significance as regards the positions where you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why was that important in terms of your actions and the steps that you took, this information that came to you from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: It was important precisely because we would never do what they did. Second, the people when they left, all of them would leave with bruises, beaten up. We would be waiting for them there to give them some help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, when you talked about this firing from the weapons that you had, when you were there what were your activities on the front line? How did things proceed there? What did you do using your weapons that you had, and what did your people do when you were the company commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the same objection. I don't see how this arises from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was talk about sniper actions, permanent sniper actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have ruled. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How did you fire from your weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: We fired infantry weapons during combat, during attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And were the screens on your side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, there were screens on our side, too, because these were passages that we used to -- to move around, in order to protect us from getting killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the building where the blind children centre was, in the last years of the war you said it was damaged. Can you describe in more detail what the damage was on the building and if anything in particular was damaged on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: There were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and I apologise for being a nuisance, but Mr. Tapuskovic asked this very question in his examination-in-chief about the damage, and now he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, you know the purpose of re-examination. It's not to reopen your case. If you have nothing more to re-examine on, I will close, I will terminate the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since a tank was mentioned during the cross-examination and the 60, 80, and 120-millimetre howitzers were mentioned, too, after the assuming of the command by Dragomir Milosevic were these weapons at Nedzarici at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: No. That was pulled back and it wasn't in Nedzarici anymore. That's what I told the Prosecutor also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. That concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal. Just a minute. Just a minute. The -- we'll have to ask you to come back because Judge Harhoff has some questions for you. Now, this morning we received the Defence response to the Prosecution's motion to exclude the testimony of a particular witness. It would be best if the Trial Chamber were to give its ruling on this during the next session, because as I understand it, the witness whose evidence may be excluded is to testify on Tuesday. We received it in the French. Regrettably, I do not speak French, but I have had made efforts to have it translated and I'm going to utilise this break with my colleague to examine the response and to deliberate on the decision that we'll give. For that reason, we'll take a longer break. We'll break for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we have the break I want to ask the Defence whether the witness T13 will be called to testify this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for coming back, Witness. You explained to me this morning when we were speaking about the line of sight from the passageway towards the school for the blind that it would be impossible to see the school from the passageway and vice versa because there would be screens.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But your subsequent testimony left some doubt in my mind as to what was actually the substance of your earlier testimony, because I'm sure that you have discovered by now that the passageway is interesting, because at this location one of the incidents took place which are covered by the indictment against the accused in this case. This is why a number of questions have related exactly to the possibility of seeing through the passageway from the school of the blind, and therefore, I wanted to ask you a more precise question to clarify the answer that you gave to me this morning, because you said that there were blankets in front of every passage so as to cover the -- to exclude the sight and thereby to cover the civilians from -- from the shooting. And therefore, my question would be do you remember for sure if there were blankets to cover, in particular, this particular passageway during the war? If you have doubts about which passageway it was exactly, I suggest that we have a look at -- at 65 ter 2860, if that might assist you in answering my question. Could we please ask the registrar to give us this picture again. I think it was Exhibit D279. Thank you. Witness, you see from the building which you have marked with "S," which I understand was the school for the blind. If you follow a straight line upwards from that building, you will see a marking consisting of one or two small red circles. Do you see that area? Do you see that mark? It's just to the left of your letter -- exactly. If the usher could put --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So this is the passageway that we're talking about. And my question to you, do you know for sure if there were screens set up also to cover that particular passage, or was that just something you assumed because you said that there were screens in front of all the passageways? If you don't remember anything particular about this passageway, then please just tell me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I recall that each passageway had covers of sorts, be it screens, containers, or anything else. Each of the passageways were covered by some means. I am certain of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall if these screens were replaced from time to time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, of course such screens were changed and replaced, because usually these were blankets or curtains. After a while they had to be changed. As to whether this one specifically was changed or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And why would they have to be changed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Those were usually blankets. They would be worn out because of the sun, the rain. They would rot away. We were doing the same thing in Nedzarici, and we had to replace them regularly. They simply rot away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. My other question was about the school of the blind, which is shown on the bottom of the picture. You see that turning towards us is the facade of the building, and my question is --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- whether you recall that any changes were made to the other facade, that is to say the facade that we cannot see from here because it is behind the building, the facade there. Do you remember if anything was changed on that facade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: That facade? Well, this what we can see here is probably the new facade, because the old one was riddled with bullets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sure. Sure. But my question is to the other facade, that is to say the facade that we cannot see on this picture, my question is do you recall if during the war any changes were made in that facade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I do not remember. They were full of holes from bullets, and part of the facades fell down, but other than that I don't remember any alterations. I'm not sure what you have in mind. I know only that it was damaged by bullets. It was full of holes. I don't know of any other changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very good. Do you know if any of those holes penetrated the facade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was full of holes, but I don't remember any large holes though. I don't know what you mean exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What I mean exactly, if you recall if there were any holes that penetrated the wall so as to enable you to look out from the inside to the outside. If you were, for instance, on the roof and there was a hole that penetrated the wall, then that would enable you to look out through that hole from the roof of the building into the open area. That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: The roof was also full of bullet holes. But as for anyone climbing up there to observe, I strongly doubt that. They didn't dare, and they tried to stay safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if it was possible to access the roof of the building from inside without being seen from the outside? That is to say, were the staircases inside the building located in such a way as to enable you to get to the roof without being exposed to the window sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: There were stairs, but anyone could be seen. If someone was going from the lower floors to the upper floors one could be seen from the outside, as the windows faced that way. One would be seen on the stairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm very sorry, but I would ask your leave to ask further questions of this witness in light of Judge -- His Honour Judge Harhoff's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, the questions from His Honour Judge Harhoff about the screens and the blankets, do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And His Honour Judge Harhoff asked you whether these blankets and screens were replaced from time to time. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that these screens and these blankets were -- and curtains were changed from time to time because they were fired at from the school for the blind and therefore became ineffective. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: Listen, as I said a moment ago to the Judge, the blankets were changed because they were run down, exposed to the sun and the rain. And it might have been because of the bullets, too, but largely it was due to the weather conditions. There was no reason for me to, for example, fire at them if I couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you accept the possibility that it could have been because of the bullets coming from the SRK side. You accept that possibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the amount of speculation is problematic as always. The witness tried to be as clear as possible when answering Judge Harhoff's questions. What we have now is an attempt to extract something from the witness whereby he is asked to speculate. He already stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I agree, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I've made my determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you also told His Honour Judge Harhoff that these -- these screens were set up in all passageways and including this passageway. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you've told the Court that when you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was never allowed to Defence during the Prosecution case. It was rejected by this very Bench on several occasions because this is cross-examination in relation to the questions asked by one of the -- one of the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I have every intention of allowing you to ask further questions, too, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not the matter at hand. I am talking about the principle. So far it has never been allowed. I wasn't thinking of posing some additional questions. I might have some, but I wasn't referring to that. This is a matter of principle. It is moving far more ahead than what the usual practice of this Bench was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, one more question and then we'll finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just recall that in the Prosecution case on occasion -- on several occasions I and my colleagues sought leave to ask questions arising from Your Honour's questions, and in that fashion the Defence was similarly allowed to cross-examine on my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's entirely true. That's entirely true, but we are not reopening the cross-examination. That's not the purpose of this exercise. Just ask one or two questions to follow up on what Judge Harhoff raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And then that's exactly what I intend to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I had asked you a question prior to my learned friend arising, and that was: You accept therefore the possibility that the curtains and the blankets could have been replaced because of the firing and the bullets, as you said, and I'm putting to you coming from the SRK side. Do you accept that possibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Robinson, again we are in the domain of speculation. I thought that there would be something new in my learned friend's question, but Mr. Sachdeva is again asking for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not allowing the question, Mr. Sachdeva. I believe that should end your recross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise, and you have ruled. I would just, with your leave and with the greatest respect, persist in -- when Judge Harhoff asked -- His Honour Judge Harhoff asked the questions about the replacement of the curtains and the blankets, it is also therefore -- the witness had given evidence that they were replaced because of weather and because of other factors, and therefore I, in my submission, do not see it's calling for speculation if I ask the witness -- if I put to the witness that there were other factors which led to the removal of the screens. I mean either than his testimony with respect to all of the reasons for removing the screens is speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that's a matter that the Chamber will have to make up its mind about. Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, one last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One last question. I think this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, we have evidence given to us by other witnesses, and we will evaluate the totality of the evidence that there's been offered to us, and that's it. I don't think there's any reason to any further in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, do you have any questions arising from Judge Harhoff's questions or from the questions raised by Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with the questions posed by the Prosecutor. His Honour Judge Harhoff received his answers. I wanted to follow up on Mr. Sachdeva's question, just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you tell us this: I have to go back to some of the questions I had already posed, but it has to do with this: Were you only firing from snipers or what did it look like? What sort of activity was there in your trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T52
utterances.text: From the trenches we opened fire from our rifles. In the case there was an attack and we were trying to defend, we fired from rifles. What sniper? We had no snipers then, and we were not allowed to fire from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't insist no any further. I believe this is sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, not another question, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, no, not another question but with respect, another submission. His Honour Judge Harhoff asked about the -- the damage or the restructuring of the building, the school for the blind, and on that specific issue I have one photograph and one question to put to the witness, with your leave. Specifically on that issue, and I submit that it does arise out of His Honour's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As much as we admire your persistence and your combative style, not overly combative, Mr. Sachdeva, we will not allow any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence and the Chamber is grateful for you coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will now give its decision on the Prosecution's motion to exclude the testimony of Witness T22, dated the 25th of June. The Defence filed their response this morning, the 28th of June. It is the Prosecution's argument that Witness T22, who was a policeman from Trnovo and worked in the police station in Kula, will testify about events in locations that are "well beyond," the geographical scope of the amended indictment and that his testimony is irrelevant to the charges in the indictment and has no probative value. The Prosecution argues that pursuant to Rules 89(C) and (D) and 90(F) the witness's evidence should be excluded. The Defence argues that the charges against the accused are based on military activities taking place within the area of responsibility of the SRK, including the municipalities of Trnovo and Novo Sarajevo, and that it is the Defence case that the intensity and geographical scope of the military activities of the ABiH precludes the existence of a campaign of shelling and sniping against civilians in Sarajevo. The Defence submits that Witness T22 is an eyewitness to military activities that took place in Trnovo and at Novo Sarajevo, and that he will testify about the military activity between the SRK and the ABiH in those municipalities. The Trial Chamber disagrees with the Prosecution's submission as to the geographical scope of the indictment. The way the case has proceeded and indeed of the evidence that has been presented indicate that Trnovo and Novo Sarajevo are within the geographical scope of the indictment. The Prosecution's motion has not satisfied the Chamber that this witness's evidence should be excluded on the ground that it is irrelevant. The Chamber will dismiss the motion, but that of course is without prejudice to the consideration that the Chamber will give to the relevance of any specific piece of evidence sought to be adduced, whether in response to an objection from the Prosecution or to a point that the Chamber takes proprio motu. The motion is dismissed. May we have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just say to the witness, Witness, you remain subject to the declaration that you made previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, last time we began this examination-in-chief, and you started your testimony. Could you now, as briefly as possible, summarise what happened to you and what this looked like until you returned to your home?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're talking about the time I spent in the JNA, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you started testifying about that, and then you started giving certain explanations, as is your right, but could you now take up your testimony where you left off and tell us as briefly as possible what all this looked like until you returned to your home?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. The situation was difficult. The Croatian forces, the National Guard Corps, and the HVO attacked the barracks, the Kalnicki Partizani barracks in September or October. I think it was September, in the second half of September. They attacked from all sides. Two days later, when they had been attacking us for two days, the JNA did not allow them to enter the barracks. Negotiations began between General Trifunovic and Colonel Popov, and a peaceful hand-over of the barracks was agreed on. The soldiers and officers were promised that nothing would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, can you tell us what happened to you, but please be very brief.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken prisoner on the 21st of September in the Kalnicki Partizani barracks, and when the HVO soldiers entered the barracks they took all our clothes off. They gave us civilian clothing, they said nasty things to us and, to be brief, as agreed they exchanged us at Sid where the border point was and then we went to the Viktor Bubanj barracks in Belgrade in Serbia and from there we were sent to our local departments from where we had been sent to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I realise we're constrained for time right now, Your Honour, but really this is very far reaching from anything to do with the case at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What does it have to do with the case at hand, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought the witness would be very brief and just say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We rule it irrelevant. We rule it irrelevant. Move and to something that is germane and pertinent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where did you arrive after being demobilised?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Sarajevo. I reported to the municipality of Ilijas, my home municipality, and I was there when the conflicts in Sarajevo began.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was your status then that of a civilian?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a civilian. The Territorial Defence, and this was in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say very briefly what happened in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second half of May 1992 I happened to be in my native area with the other population when the Territorial Defence was arming people and organising village guards, and I joined. I joined in. This went on until August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, what happened that brought about these events and your becoming part of those village guards, and what was happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as in 1992, inter-ethnic conflicts began. There were some clashes in which Muslim forces mounted intensive attacks on Serb areas inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let's be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask whether the witness is talking about his own area or is he talking about a wider geographical area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me ask him. Witness, are you speaking about the -- your area, or is it a wider area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of events in the wider area but also my area where I spent the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you join the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, or we did, in the second half of 1994. Sorry, I made an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Victims and Witnesses Unit has informed us that this witness is still not well. He decided to come here at his own risk, but he had a fever. I didn't want to insist on the witness starting his testimony today, but we were informed half an hour ago that he still wasn't feeling well. It seems to me that his situation, he's evidently a little bit confused. I think this shows that he may not be able to answer properly. We're approaching the end of today's session in any case, so can we adjourn now, because I can't believe that the witness would not be able to understand a simple question. He's speaking now of 1994, and I was asking him about 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Anybody could make a mistake like that. However, in view of the representations that you have made about the witness's health, and also in few of the fact that we are just two or three minutes away from the close, we will adjourn now, and we will resume on Tuesday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of July, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.41 p.m.,
